opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing is going to shift a lot over the next couple of years. Right now, a lot of Chinese companies, especially the big platforms like Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent, treat AI spending partly as a defensive necessity. They see what's happening in the US, with hundreds of billions going into data centers, and they feel they can't afford to fall behind. But there's also a strong cultural and business emphasis on efficiency and near-term return that you see less of in Silicon Valley, where people are comfortable burning enormous amounts of capital on a long-term bet about AGI.

What DeepSeek showed, and what labs like Qwen and Moonshot keep reinforcing, is that you can get very close to the frontier with far less compute if you're clever about the engineering. I think that's going to shape how Chinese companies think about spending. It's less about raw scale for its own sake and more about whether you can be the most efficient at training and serving, and then deploy that into products that already have hundreds of millions of users.

The export controls are a big part of this too. When you can't freely buy the best Nvidia chips, compute becomes a scarce strategic resource rather than something you just throw money at. So spending gets tied to building domestic chip ecosystems, Huawei Ascend and others, and that becomes almost a national industrial priority more than a single company's capex decision.

Over time, I expect Chinese companies to view AI spending more like infrastructure, similar to how they viewed mobile payments or cloud: something that gets woven into everything and monetized through scale and adoption, not necessarily through selling a premium model API. The open-weight strategy fits that well. You give the model away, build mindshare and developer ecosystems globally, and capture value elsewhere. So I'd say the spending will keep growing, but the justification will be much more pragmatic and product-driven than the "race to superintelligence" narrative you hear in the US.

r001.rationale: Predicts AI spending will become infrastructure like cloud, monetized through scale and adoption rather than premium model APIs.

r002.rationale: Describes spending as a defensive necessity and as support for domestic chip ecosystems, but does not clearly say companies will view it as necessary investment in building the AI technology they want.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to look pretty different from how it looks in the US, and a lot of that comes down to capital and incentives.

In the US, you've got this unusual situation where a handful of labs can raise tens of billions of dollars on the premise that scaling is going to keep paying off, and the people writing the checks are largely okay not seeing a return for years. That's just not the environment most Chinese companies are operating in. There's less of that free-flowing venture and hyperscaler money, there's real constraint on compute from export controls, and a lot of the big players are public companies or part of conglomerates where someone is asking about margins every quarter.

So what I expect, and what you're already seeing with groups like DeepSeek and Qwen, is that Chinese labs view spending through a much more efficiency-first lens. The question isn't "how big of a cluster can we build," it's "how much capability can we get per dollar and per chip." That's why you see so much emphasis on training efficiency, on inference optimization, on releasing open weights that drive adoption cheaply rather than trying to win a frontier race on raw scale. Open weights are a really rational play when you can't outspend someone but you can out-distribute them.

The other piece is that the spending is going to be more tied to products and deployment than to the pure research moonshot framing. The ecosystem there is very good at taking a capable model and pushing it into applications fast, and the companies that survive are going to be the ones that can show the spend turning into something people use. I don't think you'll see many Chinese companies trying to justify a hundred-billion-dollar training run on a story about superintelligence. They'll justify it on cost per token and market share.

Where it gets interesting is whether that constraint ends up being an advantage. If the next couple of years are more about making models cheaper and more deployable than about another order of magnitude in scale, the companies that were forced to be frugal might actually be better positioned than the ones that got used to unlimited budgets.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Chinese and US funding incentives and predicts efficiency-focused spending, but it does not compare AI spending to cloud spending versus SaaS subscriptions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses spending to improve models and support deployment, but does not clearly predict that Chinese companies will regard AI spending as a necessary investment in building the technology they want.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll increasingly see it as a strategic investment. If you’re a major Chinese technology company, you have to take seriously the possibility that AI changes your core business—search, advertising, commerce, cloud services. So even if the immediate return is uncertain, there’s a strong incentive to invest and learn.

But I’d separate spending on AI from spending on the biggest possible training run. A company can put substantial resources into making models cheaper to serve, integrating them into products, and figuring out what customers actually want. My expectation is that you’ll see both: a few companies competing at the frontier, and a much broader group asking how to turn increasingly capable models into a sustainable business.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI as a strategic investment but does not compare it with cloud spending or SaaS subscriptions.

r002.rationale: It says major Chinese technology companies have a strong incentive to invest and learn, and describes spending resources to adapt models and integrate them into products—communicating investment as necessary to develop AI capabilities for their needs.

sol-6.1.text: I think they’ll increasingly see it as a strategic investment. If AI becomes central to how you build products and run your business, you need to develop that capability, even if the immediate return is uncertain. But I’d expect companies to be selective about where they spend—training a frontier model is a very different commitment from using an existing model in a product. The question is where owning the technology gives them enough of an advantage to justify the cost.

r001.rationale: It describes AI spending as a strategic investment and distinguishes training a model from using one, but does not predict a shift toward treating it like cloud spending rather than SaaS subscriptions.

r002.rationale: It says companies will need to develop AI capability when AI becomes central to their business, and that owning the technology may justify the cost.
